A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount. Sensitive data requires strong justification and careful consideration of potential harm, focusing on equity.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for trust and effective advising. Less explainable models are less useful to us as advisors.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness cannot come at the cost of helping those who need it most. A small loss in overall accuracy is acceptable if it leads to more equitable outcomes.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach followed by the option of a meeting feels most supportive and respectful to students.
A1.notes.Q7: Personalized follow-up warrants more proactive, but wider general outreach requires caution against overwhelming students.
A1.Q8.1: It would be helpful to know more about how data security is being handled and the process for students to opt out of this system. Also how outcomes of interventions are tracked.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is key, especially with potentially sensitive data. We need to be really careful about what we collect and why. Some categories are just too risky.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust and effective advising. Students need to understand *why* they’ve been flagged, otherwise it's unhelpful. We can accept some accuracy loss.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount, even if it means helping slightly fewer students overall. Unequal impact reinforces existing inequalities - we should focus on identifying all who need support.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is much more effective, but requires advisor time. Regular check-ins are good – not too frequent to be intrusive, but often enough to make a difference.
A2.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach justifies being more selective; fewer false positives matter when there's individual advisor involvement and tailored support offered.
A2.Q8.1: It would be helpful to understand how the model handles students who transfer *into* the university with prior academic difficulties – is that factored in?

A3.notes.Q3: Protecting student privacy is paramount, but proactively reaching those who might struggle is vital. Sensitive data needs strong justification and safeguards.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for trust and effective advising. A 'black box' model wouldn’t be helpful in my role. Some loss of accuracy is acceptable.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness shouldn't mean sacrificing all effectiveness, but equity must be considered. Missing vulnerable students due to bias isn’t acceptable.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is best, but a simple email followed up with an optional meeting seems reasonable and respectful.
A3.notes.Q7: With generic emails the risk of overwhelming students is high; with personalized ones it’s more acceptable to be slightly proactive.
A3.Q8.1: It would be helpful to understand how decisions about data inclusion and model parameters will be made, and how student feedback can be incorporated.

S1.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, especially with more sensitive data. Small improvements don't justify overreach. First-gen and financial aid *might* be useful for fairness adjustments.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust & understanding *why* I was flagged. Losing accuracy to have clear reasons feels worth it, but only to a certain point.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness matters immensely; my own dropout experience highlights systemic issues. A slight dip in overall accuracy is acceptable if it means equal support for everyone.
S1.notes.Q6: Personalized contact feels more supportive than a generic message, and an invitation to talk is valuable. Twice a year feels frequent enough without being overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: I'd rather risk missing some students than spamming people with unhelpful contact. Personalized emails justify reaching out to fewer, more relevant cases.
S1.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t ask about the possibility of false positives impacting student mental health – being flagged can be stressful even if unwarranted.

S2.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, but some data helps identify those truly needing support. Nationality & first-gen status might reveal systemic issues worth addressing with fairness adjustments.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial, especially for students new to the system like me. Losing too much accuracy for it isn't worth it if only a small improvement gained.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is key, especially as an international student. Missing students from certain backgrounds isn’t acceptable, even with minor overall accuracy loss.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and more supportive than generic emails. A meeting would be good, but not constantly.
S2.notes.Q7: With personalized support, fewer false positives are acceptable. With general email, a broader net is OK to avoid missing anyone needing help.
S2.Q8.1: It would be helpful to know how the model's decisions are audited and reviewed for bias over time, beyond initial fairness checks.

S3.notes.Q3: Privacy is very important, but I’m willing to share info about my disability if it helps *everyone* get support. It feels different because of past experiences needing accommodations.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, especially for students with chronic conditions or those who've struggled before. Knowing *why* helps me trust the system and advocate if needed.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical. I’ve felt ‘othered’ in academic settings before. A slight dip in overall accuracy to ensure equitable support across groups is worth it.
S3.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and I'd likely ignore them. Personalized outreach is better, but not overwhelming. A meeting gives me agency to discuss options.
S3.notes.Q7: Personalized emails justify more selective contact. Broad emails risk being seen as spam. I'd prefer a balanced approach prioritizing quality over quantity of contacts.
S3.Q8.1: It feels like the survey assumes all data is 'safe'. There needs to be transparency about *how* privacy is protected, not just assurances that it is. Plus, what if the model misinterprets my health condition and suggests irrelevant help?

S4.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, but disability *could* help identify students who need support proactively if it improves fairness in the system. Less sensitive data feels less invasive.
S4.notes.Q4: I really value being able to understand *why* something happens, so losing that for a small accuracy gain isn't worth it. A large improvement would be needed for the lower levels of explainability.
S4.notes.Q5: It’s more important to me that the model doesn't *miss* students who need help, even if it means it isn’t perfect across all groups. Prioritizing recall feels right.
S4.notes.Q6: A generic email is too impersonal, but a phone call feels overbearing. A personalized invitation to talk feels like the best balance between outreach and respect for boundaries.
S4.notes.Q7: With generic emails, wider net is okay; but with personalised contact from an advisor, it’s important to avoid wasting their time – or mine – on unnecessary outreach.
S4.Q8.1: I'm concerned about the 'black box' aspect of these models and whether biases could be built in without anyone noticing. More transparency during development is crucial for trust.

S5.notes.Q3: I’m hesitant about sharing personal details, but understand some data might help. Nationality/first-gen status could be relevant given my experience adapting to a new system.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital, especially for students like me who are new to the Danish system. A ‘black box’ model isn't helpful; I need to understand why.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is key, even if it means fewer students are reached overall. The system shouldn’t exacerbate existing disadvantages for international or minority groups.
S5.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, and a meeting allows for a real conversation. Not too frequent, as it could feel intrusive.
S5.notes.Q7: I prefer fewer targeted contacts over many blanket emails. A personalized approach is more valuable than simply increasing the number of students contacted, especially if it’s a high-stakes intervention like one-on-one support.
S5.Q8.1: It would be good to know how often the model is reviewed and updated, to ensure it remains fair and relevant as the student population changes.

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, but some data *can* help if it's genuinely about support. Nationality & first-gen status are relevant to my experience but need careful consideration.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust. A 'black box' feels unfair, especially given my experience starting over in a new education system. I need to understand *why*.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is more important than maximizing overall identification, even at some cost. Missing vulnerable students because of bias is unacceptable. Prioritizing recall makes sense.
S6.notes.Q6: Personalized contact feels less intrusive and more supportive than a generic email. A meeting offers proper dialogue, but twice yearly seems sensible – not too much pressure.
S6.notes.Q7: Less intervention with general support feels right; personalized means contact is meaningful & potentially higher impact. Over-contact breeds resentment and mistrust.
S6.Q8.1: The model should be continually monitored for bias, and there needs to be a clear appeals process if a student believes they have been unfairly flagged. Access to Danish language help!

S7.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, especially with sensitive data. Disability info *could* be useful for fairer support, but only if it actually improves outcomes and isn’t just used to categorize.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, particularly given my dyslexia - I need to understand *why* something is happening. A big drop in accuracy for explainability isn't worth it.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness matters hugely. Missing students from marginalized groups would be unacceptable, even if it means slightly fewer total identifications. Prioritize helping those who are already falling through the cracks.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal. A personalized email or invitation to meet with an advisor seems best – more targeted and supportive.
S7.notes.Q7: With a simple notification, contacting many feels okay. But with personalized advice, fewer false positives are better - it's resource-intensive for advisors and potentially distressing if unnecessary.
S7.Q8.1: It would be good to know how the model handles students with diagnosed learning differences like dyslexia; will support be tailored or just generic?

S8.notes.Q3: I’m wary of data collection, especially around sensitive topics. Some improvement needs to be *significant* for me to accept it. First-gen status and financial aid seem less intrusive than others.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial, especially given my own experience dropping a programme. I need to understand *why* – for myself and so advisors can help properly. Less explainability isn’t worth the increased accuracy.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is important, but not at the expense of helping many students. A small decrease in overall identification to ensure equal outcomes seems reasonable. It's more important to find those who are falling through the cracks.
S8.notes.Q6: A personalized email seems least intrusive but most effective. An invitation to meet offers more support, so including that is good. Twice a year feels manageable without being overwhelming.
S8.notes.Q7: With generic outreach it's better to err on the side of caution and contact fewer, as some might resent it. With personalized options contacting a bit more is acceptable.
S8.Q8.1: I worry about the data being used for anything beyond support – are there safeguards against that? And how will this system interact with existing advisor workloads?

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is vital, especially given my own experiences with managing a long-term condition. Data collection must be minimized & used responsibly.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability builds trust and allows students to understand how help is being offered. Losing that is too high a price for minor accuracy gains.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable, but the cost can't be *too* high. It’s better to help fewer students equally than many with bias.
S9.notes.Q6: Personalized contact is better - it shows you’re seen as an individual, not a data point. A meeting offers real support too.
S9.notes.Q7: The more targeted the intervention (personalized email/meeting) the more accepting I am of reaching fewer students overall.
S9.Q8.1: It's crucial to acknowledge that predictive models can reinforce existing biases in higher education access and success. Continuous monitoring for unintended consequences is essential.
